God too is wont to be in the midst of them, and to heap up grace in those who for his sake are heaped together, are gathered, [0508D] and speak of him. Whence the bride, the more inflamed at the question concerning the beloved, begins to express his beauty and to tell the benefits conferred on her by him, saying: *My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands.* He is white, because he is the brightness of eternal light, and Light of light. White, because he is free from all sin, because he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth. And ruddy, because in his passion he was drenched with his own blood, in which there was neither beauty nor comeliness, that he might make me comely, and that his blood might adorn the cheeks of my soul, and might reform me who was deformed. Therefore is he my beloved to me, because he suffers these things for me, and does these things also for me. Who is also chosen out of thousands, because out of the whole human race none is without [0509A] sin, except him. For none is like him among the lawgivers, nor among the thousands of thousands, and the ten times a hundred thousand who minister to the Lord of majesty, or stand by him. For gold or glass shall not be made equal to him, that is, the society of the supernal citizens, whose hearts both shine with brightness and are translucent with purity to one another. And this, because he is not only man, but God. Whence follows:

*His head is the best gold.* His head is his divinity, because the head of Christ is God. Which head is the best gold, because the goodness of the divinity excels all things that were made by it; this is the gold of the land of the living, and the gold of that land is the best. For shining, so that it cannot be seen by human eyes, and by those living in the flesh. For man shall not see God, [0509B] and live. Therefore then is he my beloved, because this is his head, this his chief part, this, the sublime which cannot be seen. I shall see when that life shall have appeared, because then I shall be like him, and I shall see him as he is. Who will grant me this twin happiness, because he will configure the body of my lowliness to the body of his brightness, and will conform my soul to the likeness of his divinity.



## CHAPTER XXXVII. *On the quality of the members of the beloved.*

*His locks are as the upraised boughs of palms, black as a raven [n: (Cant. V)]*. The upraised boughs of palms are the *spatulae*, that is, the longer branches, ever tending to lofty things. The bride has expressed what the beloved is in himself; now she begins to set forth what he is in his members. Whose [0509C] locks she calls those who cleave to him in faithful service, and these she declares to be like the palm and the ravens alike. The palm below is rough, and wrapped about with tighter bark; above it is beautiful and ample, both in sight and in fruit. So the members of Christ below do hard things, and suffer adversities, and above, in the eyes of God, are beautiful and fruitful. For through the hard things of the body they purge themselves, and advance to the beauty of the soul and to spiritual sublimity. For whence they consider the supernal beauty, thence they gladly labor below. For their eyes are in their head, that is, in Christ, and in his golden head, that is, his divinity; thither they desire to reach, thither to tend, to be refreshed by his comeliness and to be irradiated by his splendor. For they sigh after that vision, after that beginning once seen, and [0509D] the days seem to them few for the greatness of love, and the tribulation light in comparison with the weight of glory. For the sufferings of this time are not worthy of the future glory of that vision. The consideration of glory and of the reward stirs up desire in them, and desire makes labors light, and carries upward. Whence therefore they consider and covet the supernal things, thence they are strengthened below; and whence they are strengthened below, thence they triumph over labors, and grow into the heights of the virtues. For the palm advances greatly by ascending on high, and holds forth victory by its own signification. The locks of the beloved are as the upraised boughs of palms, because the elect, while they ever lift themselves up to the heights of the virtues, at length through God's grace bring themselves through to victory. [0510A] In the lowest things their life is wrapped about as with many barks, while it is straitened by innumerable tribulation. But in the highest it is spread out, as with leaves of beautiful greenness, by the amplitude of the reward. Who are also called black as a raven: the blackness of the good is that they reckon themselves sinners, and bear the shame of their sins in their countenance. For they choose to be looked down upon, they bear contempt with an even mind, and mean works and a sordid habit they not only do not shun, but even seek, knowing that in this humility a precious treasure lies hid. This is the blackness of the good, in which they make themselves like to ravens, that they may be made like to Christ also. For humility is the virtue of Christ, and whoever has it will have also the likeness of Christ; and by as much as he is the blacker through it, by so much will he be the more like [0510B] to Christ, and the more humble in his own eyes. For the good are black, and despised in their own eyes, but beautiful and precious before God. And so, the locks of the beloved being described, she begins to describe his eyes, saying:

*His eyes are as doves upon the streams of waters, which are washed with milk, and sit beside the fullest floods.* The eyes of the beloved are the contemplatives, who contemplate supernal and spiritual things with the eyes of the heart. Who are as doves, because they live simply, and have a simple eye, that is, intention, so that their whole body is lightsome, that is, whatever they do or intend, they do for God's sake. They are doves also at the windows of their eyes, because they are borne toward earthly things neither by rapacity nor by love, having a dull sight in these, but in spiritual and salutary things [0510C] a sharp and clear one. This is the right eye, which, lest it scandalize us and lead us into error by harmful subtlety, cleaves continually to the documents of Scripture. And this is what is declared, that they are upon the streams of waters. Doves are wont to sit upon the streams of waters, that they may see the shadow of the hawk in the waters, and so, casting themselves upon the water, escape his talons. So the good see the shadows of the demons in Scripture, while they find there their every kind of deception, by which they are wont to deceive not only through open evils, but even through hidden ones. In which they see also that they mock now through the appearance of good, now through a false understanding, things which by the simple and by those less exercised in spiritual matters are believed sound and perfect. And so against every error or impurity [0510D] that the enemy might suggest, or that some erring and seduced man might affirm, the divine words must be looked into, and the things which are suggested or heard must be compared with these, that they may be received or confuted. For these are chaste words, silver tried by fire, proved from earthly things, and purged by the sevenfold Spirit. For whatever is consonant and agrees with the sacred Scripture which the Holy Spirit founded must be believed sound and whole, and whatever disagrees with it must be reckoned harmful. For that cannot be sound which in any way differs from the Holy Spirit. Streams too are wont to render the eyes of those who look into them clearer. So Scripture, looked into, makes the eyes of the heart more perspicacious, because the declaration of the words of God enlightens, and gives understanding [0511A] to little ones: for he who elucidates the words of God is enlightened, and is disposed to the understanding of the words of God: for the mystical senses, while they are searched out, instruct the mind, and open the sense to understanding. These doves too are washed with milk, that is, by the sweetness of their mother, grace, they are alike cleansed from sins and kept. For through spiritual consolation delight grows bitter and cheap, and earthly and carnal cleanness [cj: *munditia*; read *immunditia*, "uncleanness"] too; and through this one is pricked, so that he repents of what he has committed, and commits no others. Again, these washed doves sit beside the fullest floods. These fullest floods are the perfect joys of that life, beside which they sit, because they remove themselves from earthly delight or consolation, and study to conform themselves to the knowledge and contemplation of the supernal things, and to make them [0511B] near. For they lie down between the borders, that they may see that rest, because it is good, and the land, because it is best. They choose the utmost things of this world, because they take the supports of life for sustenance, not for pleasure, so that, dwelling thus in its borders, they may in some measure touch the borders of that life also, and lay hold of something of those joys. They lie down in the borders, because although they are here in body, there they dwell in mind, as the Apostle says: *Our conversation is in heaven [n: (Philip. III)]*. But because they use this world as though they used it not, and desire the future rest, and contemplate it in mind, they are declared to sit beside these floods. Which rest they would by no means see through contemplation, if they had not stillness of mind. Whence this sitting beside the floods [0511C] signifies their stillness, for to sit belongs to one who is still. And so, set upon the streams of waters and washed with milk, they sit beside the fullest floods, because, enlightened through Scripture, and cleansed from sins and vicious affections by the operation and sweetness of grace, they have attained stillness of mind and purity of heart. Through which two they draw a sweet draught from that living fountain, and thirst for the fountain itself, saying: *my soul hath thirsted after God, the living fountain; when shall I come, and appear before the face of God? [n: (Psal. XLI.)]* [var: Vulg. *fortem*, "the strong living God"] But those who are still imperfect and weak are not washed with this milk; because, although they have received the sweetness of consolation from God, yet not so full a cleansing alike from sins and from vices. Whence they sit [cj: *resident*; read *non resident*, "they do not sit"] beside these floods, [0511D] because they do not yet have this stillness of mind. Their sweet affection or joy is not perfect or pure, because it proceeds from a heart less cleansed. For there works together in them either natural lightness, or some prosperity, or a hidden temptation of sin. Such men through sweet affection are sometimes rolled down to the accustomed joy of carnality. For the fire of carnal concupiscence is still vehement in them through temptation, whence, cheerfulness being received, it is easily kindled, as though wood were applied. When their affection is directed toward God, it sometimes comes about that, from the occasion of places, the state, having been made lighter, is changed into a carnal one, so that, having begun with the spirit, they consummate in the flesh. Whence some in such a state suffer a motion of the flesh, or even a greater frailty. In these the sweet affection [0512A] is turned into sin. Whence, when they feel a motion of the flesh, they ought at once to draw themselves back from this sweetness, and turn to some good. For such men bitter things are more expedient than sweet, hard than soft: namely the bitterness and grief of penance, and the labor of the fight against the pleasures of the flesh, or of their own will. For harmful delight is better cured by its contrary; and sweet things, as they delight sensuality, so also make its strength. And so through hard things and labors false delight is extinguished, and stillness of mind is acquired, that there may be a sitting beside these floods, and that the supernal things may in some measure be contemplated.



## CHAPTER XXXVIII. *On the members of the beloved.*

*His cheeks are as garden-beds of spices planted by the perfumers* [0512B] [n: (Cant. V)]. The cheeks are the martyrs, who, pouring out their blood for the faith of Christ, blush as cheeks in the face of the Bridegroom. Deservedly beautiful, because they adorned the whole body of the Church, whose members they were. A great fire of love burned in them, which so inflamed them unto torments. Great was the sweetness within, which sweetened the most bitter death. This is charity, the love, namely, of God, the love of the highest good, strong as death, nay stronger than death. This had mortified in the martyrs the desires of the body, and therefore they prevailed to expose the body itself to death. Such men lived spiritually, not carnally. Now they themselves lived no longer, but Christ lived in them. Whence they could die for Christ, who lived in them, and whose spirit they had. These are the cheeks of the beloved, which blushed in the face of the militant [0512C] Church through the penalty of martyrdom, and in the triumphant Church blush with a special comeliness through the garden-bed. Which are as garden-beds of spices, and filled with virtues, which virtues after the manner of spices have alike a sweet refreshment and an odor. For the mind which they fill they refresh delightfully, and they send forth to others the odor of good repute and of example. These garden-beds are planted by the perfumers. The perfumers are the preachers, spiritual physicians, healing the languors of souls by their instruction. These have compounded a precious pigment for the faithful. a sweet draught, namely spiritual sentences with which they have steeped us. By these perfumers are these garden-beds planted, which virtues have been described by them, and written down in books, concerning which it is added:

[0512D] *His lips are lilies dropping the first myrrh.* The lips of the beloved are the preachers, because they speak his words, and announce his will. Which lips are as lilies, because they have the whiteness of innocence, and the odor of good fame. Their doctrine is beautiful, and is fragrant, because a clean life adorns and commends it. For the example of good work strengthens their preaching, and they easily persuade who accomplish in work as they teach in word. Because therefore they do what they teach, they are white and fragrant. These are the skilled physicians, first healing themselves, and taught from the remedy of their own disease to know and to heal the diseases of others. But they drop the first myrrh, when first of all they mortify themselves, and so [0513A] preach mortification to others, beginning to do, and so to teach. The first myrrh is also the penalty of martyrdom, which they drop upon the faithful, when they preach that the body is rather to be exposed to death than that one should depart from God, or commit a mortal sin. The death of Christ too is the first myrrh, which they specially preach. For he himself is the head of martyrdom, from whom martyrdom chiefly began, and through whom the faithful were strengthened to endure martyrdom. The first myrrh is the best; whence it signifies the death of Christ, which was best, because it was the redemption of the whole world. This these lips drop, that is, the preachers, and they set it before the faithful to be imitated, and always to be held in memory. This, thought upon, mitigates the goads of the flesh, extinguishes the temptations of the enemy, consoles in desperation, blots out [0513B] sins, mortifies vices, strengthens the mind, confers grace. The death of Christ, his griefs and labors, are our merits, not his own. For all the things which he did or endured, he merited not for himself, but for us. Coming also in death to the tribunal of Christ, we ought to place our confidence chiefly in his merits, and, for the evils committed or the goods omitted, to set these against the accusing enemy. And so the death of Christ is the first myrrh, the best myrrh, because it mortifies all our evils, so powerful that there is nothing so unto death, and unto eternal death, which it does not loose and quicken. There follows:

*His hands are turned on the lathe, golden, full of hyacinths.* The hands of the beloved are the works of the good, which are turned on the lathe, because they are straight and perfect. As a lathe-turning [0513C] is rolled straight and smooth, and suffers in itself nothing uneven, no obstacle; so the good work nothing reprehensible, doing nothing in which a neighbor may be offended, or scandalized, or weakened. And so the working of the good is straight and polished, because they seek heavenly things alone, not turning aside to the right or the left, but walking by the royal way. For they rule themselves, and direct themselves to that which is salutary and expedient, not to that which human cupidity seeks. They exercise themselves more where the advancement is greater, and less there where the profit is less. For many are exceedingly anxious about the least things and neglect the greater, performing works of the kind that are good, but not doing them in charity. They fortify indeed the castle of their soul with many works, [0513D] but they leave one opening for the enemy by which he may enter. Of which castle this will be the firm fortification, that a man always have the intention of not committing a mortal sin, and, if he shall have committed one, of repenting at once. And likewise the solicitude of knowing mortal sins, and of being secretly contrite for those which he is not able to know. The working of the good, therefore, is illuminated by divine wisdom. Whence these hands are called golden, because they shine through divine wisdom, and are not darkened through sin or through ignorance. They shine also before men to the glory of the heavenly Father, because they are not darkened by sins or by indiscretion, and all the things which they do are done for God's sake, and with a simple intention. Whence it is added that they are full of hyacinths, because they are done by hope and desire of heavenly things alone: for the hyacinth [0514A] is a stone of an airy and green color. These hands are full of hyacinths, because all the working of the good, every intention, seeks the supernal reward, and God's good pleasure. For this cause it grows bright after the likeness of the sapphire, and is fresh in good, that it may please God, and may enjoy God. They are full of hyacinths, therefore, so that no place lies open in them for vain praise; they do not seek it, they do not ever receive it when offered, but always look to this stone, to the heavenly beauty, to that precious pearl, and for its sake reckon all things cheap and despise them. This stone too is changed with the air; so are the good, because they are changed according to the time. For now they exercise rigor, now clemency; now they amend excesses, now they dissemble them. And these things they do not through negligence, but through discretion. For all things [0514B] have their time, and those who do not observe the opportunity of the time deprive themselves of the fruit of profit. For sometimes an evil is better tolerated than reproved. And so according to the time and the manners of men they change themselves, nor by this mutability do they become unstable, but firm and stable. Because, while they are changed that they may better bring their causes through to effect, in the things which they intend to do they always prosper, and suffer no mutability of impediment. For they change the manner, but not the mind, and the same intention remains, although not the same action. There follows:

*His belly is of ivory, set with sapphires.* The belly of the beloved is the good married, keeping themselves chastely and using this world as though they used it not. Now the elephant is a chaste animal and of a cold nature. Whence it also [0514C] signifies those who are joined, or know one another carnally, not in order to satisfy lust, but either for the sake of begetting offspring, or of avoiding incontinence. For the intention of offspring has merit; incontinence to be avoided, pardon: for matrimony excuses it; the cause of lust, damnation, because it is a mortal sin. And so married persons who serve their own pleasure are not truly the beloved's, but the possession of the devil; nor has Christ a dwelling in these, but the devil has power: as the angel taught Tobias, saying that the demon has power over those who so undertake marriage that they are at leisure for their own lust, like the horse and the mule [n: (Tob. VI)]. But the belly of the Bridegroom is set with sapphires. The sapphire is a stone having the appearance of a serene [0514D] sky. Whence it signifies the good married, who are steeped in heavenly disciplines, meditate on the supernal things and have a taste for them. These are set with sapphires, because amid worldly acts they do heavenly works also. For although they are divided, so that they think on the things that are of the world, how they may please their spouse, they nonetheless think on heavenly things, and how they may please their Maker. This is the setting of the sapphire, that walking in the flesh they war not according to the flesh, but their conversation is in heaven



## CHAPTER XXXIX. *A description of certain members of the beloved, and the praises of the Virgin Mary.*

*His legs are columns of marble, which are founded upon bases of gold [n: (Cant. V)]*. These are they who support religious men out of their own goods, who impart temporal things to them, that they may receive spiritual things from them. For he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive [0515A] the reward of a prophet. He who supports a just man for the serving of God shall not only be a sharer of his reward, but shall have his reward together with him. These are the legs of the Bridegroom, because these are they who go about visiting the sick, and coming to those who are joined to them in the flesh; of these, not only does the door lie open to the traveler, as with Job, but they also go with Tobias to the natives, and divide to each one out of their means as they are able. Who, like columns of marble, are upright in knowledge and in work, and unbreakable by vices and sins. They are wise rightly and soundly, supplanted by no false doctrine or religion. For some teach false things under the appearance of religion. [0515B] Demons also suggest in the heart a false justice, and a false understanding in place of the light of truth. Certain men indeed bend the bow of Scripture, and prepare their arrows in their quiver, that with their arrows they may shoot in the dark at the upright of heart; and the things which the Lord has perfected, that is, has perfectly made, and has set forth above the teachers, they destroy and bend to their own error. Demons also work certain subtle things and certain revelations in some men. And likewise certain new and unwonted things, which the curious and the simple marvel at and venerate. The understanding of the good, therefore, is right and sound; their works are formed as the life proceeds out of the heart. They make straight steps with their feet, because they do all things with counsel, and they lay open in confession [0515C] not only their sins, but also the hidden suggestions of the heart. For he cannot err who lives with counsel, nor be deceived by the enemy who uncovers his suggestions. Again, the good are upright and unbroken, who are not bent that demons may pass over them, as it is written of the evil one: *Bow down, that we may pass over [n: (Isa. LI)]*. Nor are they broken by injustice, so as to consent to the temptations of demons and to fall into sin. They are therefore upright and erect, because they both keep justice in themselves, and raise themselves up for the desiring of justice and set themselves against injustice. Whose firmness and constancy is compared not to any stones whatever, but to marble, because it is not cheap and common, but precious and rare. Nor is the strength of stones their strength, because they have not grown hard through insensibility, but through the rightness of zeal. [0515D] These columns are founded upon bases of gold, that is, upon the faith of the prophets and of the apostles. For indeed the same faith was in the prophets and in the apostles. What those believed would come, these believed had come; what those hoped for and awaited, these beheld and possessed. Whence one of them speaks, saying: *My days have been swifter than a runner; they have fled away, and have not seen good [n: (Job IX)]*. These bases were golden, because they shone through works. For without works faith is idle, but through works it is precious and to be compared to gold, because it is informed by charity. Upon these bases are founded these legs and columns, because the merciful and the upright are built up upon the foundation of the prophets and of the apostles, Christ Jesus himself being the chief corner stone, [0516A] who joined two walls in himself, namely the Jews and the gentiles, the just and converted sinners, and has made men fellows of the angels in heaven. There follows:

*His beauty is as of Lebanon.* These are the virgins, having the comeliness and the likeness of Christ. For the soul which has charity has the likeness of Christ, and, advancing more fully in the correction of manners, more fully receives this likeness. When anyone has repented, straightway in the very contrition of the heart he receives the likeness on God's part, which little by little he will possess more fully, and in the future perfectly. By this likeness all the good are conformed to Christ, but more especially the virgins, who together with this likeness have the whiteness and the cleanness of life; whence it is compared to Lebanon, which signifies Christ, who is interpreted *white*; therefore cleanness is nearest [0516B] to the author of cleanness. Whence, because the virgins obtain this special comeliness, they are well called beauty. And because they are without the stain of pollution, they are more familiarly joined to the Lamb without stain. They also follow the Lamb whithersoever he shall go. They follow specially him to whom they have specially made themselves like. To live in the flesh beyond the flesh is a heavenly life, not an earthly one. Whence, when virgins tame the sin of the flesh, which above all prevails over the human race and clings to nature, in a certain manner they are outside the flesh and are made like to God, who is Spirit. They are therefore the beauty of Christ as the beauty of Lebanon. For Lebanon is Christ, nor is he only white, but also a whitening. For he makes the elect white and comely. Lebanon also is fruitful in noble trees; so Christ brings forth noble ones, [0516C] namely those whom he had regenerated through his Spirit into liberty, that they may be sons of God and truly free, that they may not commit sin, that they may not be servants of sin. Among these trees the loftier and nobler was the blessed Virgin, who was exalted like a cedar in Lebanon, that is, in Christ, because she is not lofty through herself, but through Christ, and was made lofty and chosen by him, so that she might thus grow up and herself give increase to her own Creator. A lofty and noble tree, which brought forth this lofty fruit, namely the Son of God. Finally, she is herself the cedar which grew in Lebanon, that is, in Christ; and while she herself begot Christ, the cedar as it were produced Lebanon, and the mountain came forth out of the tree when God came forth out of man. This is the new and unheard-of thing which [0516D] God did upon the earth, that a cedar should bring forth Lebanon, a tree a mountain, that a woman should compass a man, that is, God, and that him whom the world could not contain the Virgin should enclose in her womb. And so the virgins are the beauty of Christ, but the blessed Virgin is his special beauty, who never stained her beauty by any mortal or venial sin. Whence the heavenly King desired her beauty, and, taking flesh in her, adorned this beauty yet more, because he filled her with an ampler grace. And so, when the world was wrapped in darkness and deformed, he brought forth the Sun of justice, beautiful in form above the sons of men, and thus restored light for blindness, and a beautiful beauty for deformity. She therefore, singularly the beauty of Christ, beautiful above all, and most like to Christ, not only [0517A] having herself the beauty of Christ, but also restoring it in others. And so Mary is above men, in that she never committed sin, as men do, among whom none has been found who does good and does not sin. She is also above the angels, because she surpasses them in purity, while she contemplates the divinity more clearly than they. And she not only did not commit sin, but also blotted out the sins of others; nor was she only bright in herself, but also sent forth rays of light from herself, because through her the world received the light of grace. And so Mary is the middle and the mediatrix between things divine and things human, so that she surpasses human things, while she works things so lofty through her Son. O wonderful dignity, that from a woman there should proceed a sun enlightening the world, that light should shine out from earth, that through a woman the darkness of the world [0517B] should brighten into light! Through her that sun shone out of her upon the world, and gave a brighter light, because it more fully illumined hearts. Thus the eternal light rose new out of the temporal, and spread its rays more widely. Nor was the light of grace given through her on earth only, but also the vision of God to souls in heaven. This blessed one is that great sign in heaven, a woman clothed with the sun, because the sun of divinity shines in upon her, and shines round about her, and occupies her wholly, and after her, who is most of all enlightened, gives light to the citizens of heaven. She first, and above all, received the splendor of this sun. She is clothed with this sun, and is perfectly and pre-eminently flooded with the enjoyment of the divinity. And she as it were put it on, when she received so great a fullness of it. But she is clothed with this [0517C] sun in heaven for this reason, because on earth she had perfectly put on Christ, as the Apostle says: and she was *full of grace* [n: (Luc. I)]. But the moon is under her feet, that is, the Church triumphant, because it is lower, and, enlightened by this sun after her, the moon suffers a waning; and therefore, because every man except her has had some waning, he can be enlightened by this sun, but not equally clothed. This blessed one has been exalted like a cedar, has been made lofty like Christ, and if as much [cj: *tantum*; read *non tantum*, "not so much"] as Christ: Christ was the least in the kingdom of heaven, that is, in the present Church; Mary was the humblest of all who have been upon earth. Therefore she was made lofty unto this, that she might conceive the highest of all, and after him become the highest of all. Well had she humbled herself with Christ, who was to be made lofty with Christ. As [0517D] Christ is at the right hand of the Father, so is she at the right hand of the Son. Christ is above all the works of his hands; Mary is above those same works after Christ, because she has been exalted not only above the souls of the saints, but also above the choirs of the angels. In the most humble Mary, therefore, Christ humbled himself unto the taking of flesh, and thus exalted her humbled with himself. Lofty therefore is Mary, but loftier is Christ. Whence of him there follows:

*Chosen as the cedars.* To the beauty, the strength, the loftiness and the fragrance of the cedars all the glory of the woods yields; so neither the highest men on earth nor the angels in heaven can be made equal to Christ. I wish therefore to consider how lofty and pre-eminent he is in himself, and how greatly he humbled himself for my sake: whence, when [0518A] I fear the judge, I wish to consider the brother, and the partner of my nature. For he will judge in the humanity which he mercifully took for us. Let him bear the sentence of humanity and of mercy, of a brother, and not of a judge or of justice. If I shall wish to justify myself, let him be judge, and let him condemn me; if I confess myself wretched, let him bestow mercy. I myself wish to be judge in the judge's place, that he himself may not be judge, but a brother in the judge's place; and I wish to judge myself, lest he himself judge. If I come so to the judgment, and have with me in my cause the mother of mercy, who shall deny that the judge is favorable? Mary was made the Mother of God because of mercy; and this too I believe that she exercises unceasingly for the human race before the Father and the Son, and most of all will exercise this judgment in the judgment for those to be examined. [0518B] She is the gate in which Christ, the husband of the Church, will be noble, when he shall sit to judge with the senators of the earth. Then the loftiness of this cedar will appear, and how greatly he stands out above men, and how exalted he was reckoned, whose breath was in his nostrils, that is, breathed in the mouth of men. Let us therefore seek Mary, the mother of mercy and the gate of heaven, and let us hope for mercy in the gate of judgment, that through the gate of judgment we may enter unto eternal life.



## CHAPTER XL. *On Christ and his merits.*

*His throat is most sweet, and he is wholly desirable [n: (Cant. V)]*. The throat of the Bridegroom is his inward savor, and spiritual consolation, which sweetly affect those who taste and have experience of them. [0518C] For if by thinking thou comprehend the goodness of God, and, reaching unto the savor of him, thou wilt proclaim with the bride the sweetness of this throat. The taste also of his love is so sweet that it not only refreshes the mind, but even makes one forget the food of the body. If thou also contemplate spiritual and mystical things, whatever thou hast been able to comprehend of him thou wilt approve as sweet and delightful, so much so that thou wilt reckon all things except him but little sweet, nay none at all, and wilt judge that he alone is good, that he alone is to be embraced and loved. But if thou pass over in mind to the considering of things above, it will be sweet to meditate what it is to see God, and to be satisfied with the vision of him, that he himself is in us, and we in him, and that we are one with him, and to lack all misery, and to rejoice with him without end: the inward savor of these things [0518D] is the throat of the Bridegroom. But the heart which shall perceive this sweetness must be cleansed of vicious affections, because unless the vessel of the heart be pure, it less perceives, or retains, this sweetness of the spirit, because it has thus far drawn near out of the dregs of carnality. Let it therefore refuse to be consoled save in God; let it be mindful of God, and be delighted in him, and be exercised in this delight, so that his spirit may fail, that is, his own will, and that he may despise what delights outside God. As much as he shall have despised outward delights, so much will he be able to be delighted in God. Let him cast away the delight of worldly things; let him leave the world, that is, worldly things; let him approach the solitude of the mind; let him sit solitary, and let him lift himself above himself, let him lift the body above the body, that he may transcend bodily things, and comprehend the things above and the spiritual. All that is [0519A] in the world is concupiscence of the flesh, or concupiscence of the eyes, or pride of life. He who shall have despised these things, by vanquishing carnal concupiscence, by calling himself back from outward things to inward and invisible things, and by humbling himself with pride trodden underfoot, assuredly leaves the world and comes to solitude, so that he may be able to lay hold of the acquaintance and the savor of spiritual things. This is the Egypt out of which the people of God goes forth, and this is the solitude to which it ought to strive. Out of this solitude messengers are sent, and they bring back of the fruits of the land of promise. These messengers are spiritual meditations and holy desires. These are sent by the devout soul to consider this land. These, by searching out this land, enter it; they bring word of its abundance and sweetness; they carry of the fruit with them. This fruit is [0519B] the taste of that sweetness, the foretaste of that sweetness, a fruit sweet to the throat of the devout soul that tastes this fruit and experiences its sweetness. He who tastes this sees, that is, knows, how sweet is this most sweet throat of the Bridegroom, which not only excels all sweetness, but even expels it. The more the sweetness of this is felt, the more it is desired. It has hunger in this life, not satiety; refreshment, not fullness. For it is so sweet that it is always desired, so immense that it is never comprehended to the full; and he who is so affected as to call himself satisfied, and wholly filled, I know not whether he is refreshed from the throat of the Bridegroom, or from adultery and a false messenger: *They that eat me shall yet hunger,* says the Wisdom of God; *and they that drink me shall yet thirst [n: (Eccli. XXIV)]*. Here the goodness of God is a slender taste, [0519C] in the future satiety, wherewith we shall be satisfied when his glory shall be made manifest, and we shall be filled with the good things of the house of the Lord. The true savor is thus discerned from the false, because it is not vehement or impetuous; it does not titillate the flesh, but restrains and mitigates the motions of the flesh. It is modest, tranquil, light, sweet, peaceable; it strengthens the spirit, weakens the flesh, kindles and enlightens the mind; it does not lift up, but humbles. For its sweetness stirs up desire, and while it kindles ampler desires it always renders a man humble concerning his own advance. For since what he has is little, as he always reckons himself needy, so he always thinks humbly of himself. An imperfect or false savor shows a man rich to himself, because it does not penetrate unto the knowing of the riches of the goodness of God. But that savor is [0519D] imperfect which the new and the carnal as yet receive, and those who have not yet attained the perfect cleanness of the heart, but have the eyes of the heart bleared, so that they cannot see clearly, and comprehend spiritual things. Thence therefore they think themselves rich, whence they see little, and have not the true knowledge. If such men, being more enlightened, knew more, and laid hold of the immensity of this sweetness, they would rather be humbled than lifted up, because they would understand how scant is what they were able to perceive of it. False is the savor which the enemy works, and which sweetly affects and gladdens the mind; but it lifts up, it does not humble; it counterfeits fullness, but has it not: for how empty of true grace those are who perceive this will be plain if they be tried by adversities. Whence they may be compared to a bridal chamber [0520A] which is shining without, but empty within; such men shine and glitter outwardly, because they have a certain appearance of devotion, but within they are empty of virtues and have no fervor. In the secret place of this bridal chamber the enemy sleeps and has stillness, because holy desires and fiery prayers do not rouse or put him to flight, but the lukewarmness of the mind and the false brightness of religion endures him and cherishes him. Their glory is not from within, nor is it so much in conscience as in outward repute; and because they are poured out outwardly, therefore they do not know or perceive inward things. Their savor, even if it be sweet, yet is not most sweet, because it is not from the Bridegroom, but from the adversary. Most sweet is that which the good perceive, who through cleanness of heart have come to the true acquaintance of his goodness. These can proclaim his most sweet [0520B] throat, because, experience teaching them, they have tasted his sweetness. If we also consider his humanity, most sweet was his throat, through which the words of the divinity came forth, because they were spirit and life, as he himself says. Sweet therefore was the preaching, and those words with which he spoke of the kingdom of God. Most sweet therefore was his throat, and he wholly desirable: desirable was the vision of his humanity on earth, but much more desirable his glorified humanity in heaven, which is desirable even to the angels, who desire to look into it. For he is desirable in countenance, whose countenance the whole company of the citizens above desires; but most desired of all is the contemplation of his divinity, to which all that is desired cannot be compared. He is therefore [0520C] wholly desirable, who is also desirable in his members, alike in those still sojourning on earth and in those reigning in heaven, because their grace delights as much as their glory considered. For here they have the brightness of holiness, and there of glorification. Their holiness is beloved for imitating, and their joy for rejoicing with them and enjoying together with them. Sweet is the contemplation of their joy, which we hope will be ours also, and which we await. This awaiting has gladness, so that we may be rejoicing in hope of this, and patient in tribulations, or in the labors which we bear for this. Christ is therefore desirable even in his own, because out of his own glory and comeliness he made them comely and desirable, so that he may be desired not only for his own sake, but [0520D] for the sake of the elect, whom we shall have as companions and partners with him in glory, and in whose glory we shall rejoice. He is therefore wholly desirable, because in himself and in his members. And this is my beloved, O daughters of Jerusalem; this is he by whom I am loved and whom I love, not in word, nor with a human tongue, but in work and in truth, because I hear his commandments and keep them. Consider the beauty of him, desire his love, O daughters of Jerusalem, that is, souls desiring to come to the vision of the peace above: for through his love, and the fulfilling of his commandments, one comes through to the vision of his beauty, to the happiness and peace above, to which may Jesus Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, deign to lead us, who lives and reigns world without end. Amen.



## CHAPTER XLI. *The Bridegroom invites the bride to receive her inheritance.*

[0521A]

*Come into my garden, my sister, my bride [n: (Cant. V)]*. Thou hast been made a garden for me, O soul, by working in thee for me the diverse perfumes of the virtues and of good work. Now also it is time that thou come into my garden, to receive the delights of my garden, because thou art a sister, thou art an heir; come to the inheritance, because thou art a bride; come to the embraces, come to sleep that thou mayest receive the inheritance; because, when I shall have given sleep to my beloved, this is their inheritance. Thou hast slept outwardly, but thou hast watched with thy heart and hast thought upon the inheritance; come to the joy for which thou hast labored, rest after labor, contemplate by sight what thou hast contemplated by faith. [0521B] Hope has refreshed thee; let vision now refresh thee. In the left hand thou hast been still; let the right hand embrace thee, and let earthly things not constrain thee and encompass thee; come into my garden. My garden is a garden of delights. In my garden the roses of the martyrs are red with wondrous comeliness; with wondrous whiteness the lilies of the confessors and of the virgins shine and give forth their fragrance. In my garden there are kinds of diverse fruits, and as many delights as there are merits of the blessed who reign in the kingdom. In my garden is every planting of the ancient Fathers, or of the new grace. Whatever was ever planted, whatever of good has been done from the beginning of the world, hither the fruit of all has ascended. Hither it has finally come; all these things have profited thee, they await thee, they will receive thee. This is the fruit of my elect, which always remains, and is not only the fruit of those who do it, but also of those who love it in [0521C] others; by loving it thou hast made it thine, for by loving me thou hast loved all that is mine; by loving thou hast made thine things mine, and the merits of my own are common to my elect. For single things are not only of single men, but all things are of all. Come therefore hither, to receive all things at once, because all things have been prepared for thee: new things with old have I kept for thee, namely the ancient and the recent merits of my own, that thou mayest be delighted with all, mayest possess all, mayest be satisfied out of all. I have reaped my myrrh with my spices: I reaped myrrh in the martyrs, spices in the confessors and in those who lived well. The myrrh of the martyrs has come to the harvest: for their bitterness passes away, and they have come through to the fruit; for they have received the rewards for their labor. The confessors, from the confession of their own [0521D] sins and of my praise, have passed over to confessing to my name unto praise without labor, unto the praise of peace and of the vision of me. The confessors were spices: for by the example of a good life they refreshed others and were fragrant with a good odor. My myrrh also have I reaped: for I consummated the bitterness and the punishment of my death, but through this I obtained for my members the sweet joys of salvation. The tastes of whose passion are savory to me through love, but that which is confected out of it, with the sweet spice of the redemption of man, refreshes me; neither the myrrh of the martyrs nor the spices of the confessors would have perceived these joys, if the myrrh of my death had not perceived them. My blood extinguished the flaming sword set before paradise; and this being extinguished, the cherubim also, whom it barred along with itself, does not deny to man [0522A] the entrance, since he knows him to have been redeemed by the blood of his own Creator. Nor does he receive him only into his own fellowship, but also unto the likeness of knowledge; for the cherubim is called *the fullness of knowledge*, and man receives the likeness of knowledge, that he may know perfectly, and even as he has been known, who here knew by experience. I have eaten the honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk. In the passion I bore my bitter things, but now I perceive the sweet things of the resurrection. Then roasted as a fish, now I eat the honey of glorified humanity. And I who was as one despised and the last of men am now crowned with glory and honor and set above all the things of the Father, and not only above all the things of men, but also of angels; I eat the honeycomb with the honey, because in glorified humanity I enjoy in [0522B] myself the glory of the divinity, and in my members I perceive the same. This is my sweetness, these my delights with the sons of men, these the feasts, this the banquet. This is food and drink to me, that I eat these things more sweetly than honey, and drink them more pleasantly and delightfully than wine and milk. In these delights I take my joy, and with the same I feed and give drink to my members: for the honeycomb of honey were to me those sweet in manners and in works, the wine and the milk the wise and the simple; to which banquet come, O sister and bride, after thy labors.

## CHAPTER XLII. *On the assumption of Mary, and her praises.*

*Who is this that ascends, and crossing the deserts? [n: (Cant. III)]* [var: Vulg. Cant. 8:5 *de deserto*, "out of the desert"; Cant. 3:6, which the note cites, *per desertum*, "through the desert"]. Whither does she tend, or what does she portend, covered with flowers? *Papae,* filled with riches, she does not run upon the thief, the singular virgin. O robber, now art thou robbed, made the prey [0522C] of a virgin! This is the enemy of Holofernes, the Hebrew woman, why dost thou spurn the Jews, Aman, Esther is a Jewess, thou spreadest a cross for Mardochai, thou shalt be punished with it. The singular wild beast; the king is Assuerus, Esther of great name. This is that rod of Jesse, which Isaias reports to have been born of the root, whose flower is the Messiah, the harvest of whose passion has strewn the ways of the world with fruit a hundredfold, with sixtyfold and thirtyfold. This is that Sunamite who served David. This Jahel, so tiny, crushed Sisara. This is the queen of Saba, who came to the realms of king Solomon, whose wisdom she heard in the sanctuary; she saves her male child out of the hand of Pharaoh; this is the fleece of Gedeon, enriching the little vessel with dew; this is the singular *ferculum* of the true Solomon, and the ivory tower, [0522D] golden, shining from the whole, wholly delightful; this is she in whom the king reclines himself, the reclining-place of wayfarers while he turns aside; this is the inn, the King of eternal glory inclines his head upon her, having no hut. O of how sweet a memory is a mother so praiseworthy! This is the tree set aflame, but that knows not how to be burned up; the star begotten of Jacob, the herald of the true sun; the gate always barred, passable to the king alone; but also the ark of the covenant, borne upon the shoulders of David, carried over with great jubilation. She, holding the moon beneath her sole, stands compassed with the sun; such does she stand forth, and so holy, having so many charisms, so many figures, signs so great, bearing so many riddles, as there are stars of heaven. Consider how great she is, thou whoever thou art in jubilation: propped up with these little flowers, hedged about with these apples, she stands plucked out of perils, laurelled in the harbor, and, blessed, joined to the Trinity, she now enjoys the longed-for [0523A] kisses! O let the reborn now applaud! O the jubilation wherewith she jubilates, the mother made one with her son! O how brightly she glows red, clothed in double garments; the translator does not so winnow it, faith so alleges, that she now reigns with God! Hail, Mary, full of grace; may God be with thee. Of our corruption, which the Jew dreams. Let the seducer Sadducee waste away in his deceit: [0524A] for thou hast truly risen. O sweet mother of Christ, have mercy on the guilty! Hail, Mary, mother of grace, queen of the world, mother of mercy, save us from ruin, fountain of life, vein of pardon; hasten then to come when we draw near to death, that with thee we may be able to rejoice perpetually. Amen.
